title: The Baal Shem Tov
hookLine: Israel ben Eliezer, an eighteenth-century teacher in Podolia, taught that God is found in joy and simple devotion

lines: A VILLAGE, THREE HUNDRED YEARS AGO.
cards: A village in what's now Ukraine, about three hundred years ago. Most of the Jews there are poor: farmers, innkeepers, peddlers, wagon drivers. Many can barely read the prayers, let alone a page of Talmud.
The great scholars are far away, and sometimes what people hear is that real closeness to God belongs to the learned. Then a man starts walking from village to village with a very different message.
His name was Israel ben Eliezer. People came to call him the Baal Shem Tov.

teach.b: Baal Shem Tov means master of the good name; people often shorten it to the Besht. He lived in the 1700s, in the region called Podolia, and settled in the town of Medzhybizh. He wrote almost nothing himself.
What we know comes through his students, and through a book of stories about him printed decades after his death, so it's hard to say where history stops and legend starts.
His message, as his students taught it, fits in a sentence.
God is everywhere, in every place and every moment, so every moment can be a way to God. Not only study and prayer, but eating, working, walking, talking with a neighbor. And the way in is joy.
He's remembered for teaching that sadness shuts the heart, and that a person should serve God joyfully.
His followers pointed to a line from the Psalms: "Serve the LORD with gladness." The movement that grew from his teaching is called Hasidism, and its followers Hasidim.
Hasid is an old word, from the Hebrew chesed, loving-kindness; in the Psalms a hasid is a devoted, faithful one.

Not everyone welcomed the movement at first; some leading rabbis, called Mitnagdim, opposed it strongly. Within a few generations the fiercest fighting had faded, and today both are part of Orthodox Jewish life.
For the next weeks: Hasidic stories, short, surprising, and full of joy.

how: Hasidic communities today, such as Chabad, Satmar and Breslov, follow teachings that trace back to the Baal Shem Tov, and joyful song and dance, the niggun, are central to their prayer and gatherings.

o: a rabbi who opposed the new movement of joy
a devoted one, from the Hebrew for loving-kindness
a scholar who has mastered the whole Talmud

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

games.q: you're a poor wagon driver who can barely read the prayers. what does the Baal Shem Tov teach you?
o: closeness to God is only for scholars.
serve God with joy, in every moment.
games.why: he taught that God is everywhere, and that joy and simple devotion open the way, for anyone.

practice: A look back at this week: Kamtza and Bar Kamtza, give me Yavneh, the white face, peace over precision, most from my students, a page a day.

Now think of one ordinary task ahead of you, dishes, the commute, folding laundry, answering email, and picture doing it with a little joy on purpose: humming, noticing the warm water, being glad your hands work.
Not pretending it's thrilling, just letting gladness in.

wordCard.voice: Hasid. A devoted one, from chesed, loving-kindness. The followers of the Baal Shem Tov, who taught that God is found in joy.

orig.note: Hebrew: a devoted, pious one, from chesed, loving-kindness.

carryVoice: Your line: serve with joy. Every moment can be a way in, even the dishes. Until tomorrow.
